passage: Sunday night. Group project due Friday and I have written the whole report again. Shreya said "I'll do slides" and sent nothing. The other two just react with thumbs-up. I felt so resentful that I nearly typed a long message in the group chat. Instead I decided to be practical. Tomorrow I will post a list with each person's part and a day, and ask everyone to update by Wednesday. If I had set roles at the start, that was my miss too. If nothing moves, I will tell our teacher before the deadline, not after. I am tired but calmer. 🙂 Manjula

qa.q: What did Shreya say they would do?
What did Manjula feel and want to do when nobody helped?
qa.a: Manjula felt so resentful that Manjula nearly typed a long message in the group chat, but chose a practical plan instead.

qa.q: What could Manjula do if the group still does not move?
qa.a: Tell the teacher before the deadline, not after, as Manjula plans, after posting the list of parts and days.

qa.q: How might Shreya see Manjula's list of parts and days?
qa.a: Shreya may see it as a clear, fair request, or feel a little caught out about the slides, but it gives a way to start.

grounding: A groupmate carries the load while others do little and sets roles and check-ins and raises it before the deadline.

passage:
Last semester, in our four-person marketing project, I did almost everything. Jagdish missed three meetings and sent "will do tonight" messages that never turned into anything, and the other two did the bare minimum. I stayed up till 3 a.m. the night before submission, finishing his section and seething.
We got an A. Jagdish thanked everyone equally in the class group. I didn't reply. I felt like a fool.
This semester, in a new project with him again, I did it differently. At the first meeting I said, "Let's write down who does what, with dates." We did, in a shared doc. A week before each deadline I sent a check-in: "Where are we on sections?" When Jagdish hadn't started ten days before his part was due, I called him instead of quietly redoing it. "Your section's due Friday. Can you do it, or should we split it differently?"
He was embarrassed. He did it. Late on Thursday, but he did.
— Tenzin

qa.q: How many meetings did Jagdish miss last semester?
How did Tenzin feel after Jagdish thanked everyone equally?
qa.a: Like a fool, resentful after doing almost everything alone.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do differently this semester?
qa.a: Wrote down roles and dates at the first meeting, sent check-ins a week before deadlines, and called Jagdish ten days early instead of silently redoing the work.

qa.q: How did Jagdish react to Tenzin's call?
qa.a: He was embarrassed and finished his section, late on Thursday.

grounding: Shows carrying the load for free-riding groupmates, and learning to set roles early, check in and raise it before the deadline.

passage:
Tutor's note, second-year sociology, group project check-in, 9 February
In today's check-in it was clear that Maria has written most of the group's field report. The shared document's history shows her edits on eleven of fourteen pages. Hansa, assigned the interview section, has added two paragraphs in three weeks.
Before I could raise it, Maria asked to speak. She said calmly, "I want to flag that the work isn't evenly split, and I'm worried about the deadline. Can we reassign sections now?" She didn't name Hansa or sound bitter. Hansa went quiet, then said she had been struggling with the interview transcriptions and was embarrassed to ask for help.
We reset the plan: Hansa will finish two interviews by Friday using Maria's template, and the group will meet again on Monday. I have asked each member to note their contribution at the end of the report.
I will check the document on Friday.

qa.q: On how many pages does the history show Maria's edits?

qa.a: The uneven split of work and the approaching deadline.

qa.q: How did Maria raise the free-riding well?
qa.a: Calmly and before the deadline, without naming or blaming Hansa, asking to reassign sections.

qa.q: What was going on for Hansa?
qa.a: She was struggling with the interview transcriptions and was embarrassed to ask for help.

grounding: Illustrates one groupmate carrying the load and raising it politely before the deadline, leading to reset roles and check-ins.
